title: The Expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq
subtitle: The Wells of Al-Muraysi and the Poison of Tribal Discord
summary: The expedition against Banu al-Mustaliq, the water dispute and the words 'Leave it, for it is foul' in Bukhari 4905, Ibn Ubayy's saying in that report, and the classical account of Juwayriyyah. Hawazin and Bukhari 2584 are a different event and are not used.

sections.text: The Threat at the Well of Al-Muraysi

In the sixth year of the Hijrah (Sha'ban 6 AH), alarming intelligence reached the Prophet ﷺ that Al-Harith ibn Abi Dirar, the chieftain of the Banu al-Mustaliq—a prominent branch of the Khuza'ah confederacy inhabiting the Red Sea coastal corridor—was mobilizing a substantial tribal coalition to attack Madinah. Buraidah ibn al-Husayb was dispatched on a covert reconnaissance mission, successfully infiltrating their assembly and verifying their hostile mobilization.

The army met Banu al-Mustaliq at al-Muraysi'. The classical sirah describes a short fight, and it gives counts of the dead and of the captives, including Juwayriyyah bint al-Harith. Those counts are not in Bukhari 4905. Bukhari 4138 confirms that the companions went on this expedition and that captives were taken. Its subject is a question about withdrawal during intercourse. This chapter does not narrate that question, and it does not use 4138 as the source of the water dispute.

While the army was encamped around the well of Al-Muraysi, a seemingly trivial domestic altercation threatened to ignite devastating communal strife. Jahjah ibn Sa'id al-Ghifari, an employee of Umar ibn al-Khattab representing the Muhajirun, jostled over access to the water trough with Sinan ibn Wabar al-Juhani, an ally of the Khazraj representing the Ansar. Tempers flared into physical scuffles. Jahjah shouted: 'O Muhajirun, help!' while Sinan cried out: 'O Ansar, help!'

Bukhari 4905 reports that a man of the Muhajirun and a man of the Ansar quarreled and each called out for his own people. The Prophet said, 'What is this call of the days of ignorance? Leave it, for it is foul.' The sirah names the two men Jahjah ibn Sa'id and Sinan ibn Wabr. Those names are not in this Hadith.
The Treason of Abdullah ibn Ubayy

Observing the tension, Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, the hypocrite chieftain who had accompanied the campaign solely in search of plunder, seized upon the incident to incite bitter sedition among his Ansar kin. He raged: 'Have they truly done this? They have crowded us in our own land! By Allah, the parable of us and these destitute refugees (the Muhajirun) is nothing other than the ancient saying: "Fatten your dog and it will devour you!" By Allah, when we return to Madinah, the most honorable will certainly expel the most vile!'

Zayd ibn Arqam, an astute young Ansari youth sitting in the gathering, overheard Ibn Ubayy's treasonous speech and reported it faithfully to the Prophet ﷺ. When confronted, Ibn Ubayy swore solemn false oaths by Allah denying he had ever spoken the words. Umar ibn al-Khattab urged: 'O Messenger of Allah, permit me to strike off the neck of this hypocrite!' The Prophet replied with sublime forbearance: 'No, Umar; lest people say that Muhammad kills his own companions.' Divine revelation in Surah Al-Munafiqun soon descended, vindicating Zayd's honesty and exposing Ibn Ubayy's deceit.

يَقُولُونَ لَئِن رَّجَعْنَا إِلَى الْمَدِينَةِ لَيُخْرِجَنَّ الْأَعَزُّ مِنْهَا الْأَذَلَّ ۚ وَلِلَّهِ الْعِزَّةُ وَلِرَسُولِهِ وَلِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَلَٰكِنَّ الْمُنَافِقِينَ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ
'They say, "If we return to Madinah, the more honorable will surely expel therefrom the more vile." But to Allah belongs all honor, and to His Messenger, and to the believers, but the hypocrites do not know.' (Surah Al-Munafiqun 63:8)

To extinguish the toxic atmosphere, the Prophet ﷺ ordered the army to march immediately at the peak of midday heat—a time when travelers invariably rested. He kept the troops marching without pause throughout the entire day, through the night, and into the scorching heat of the following noon until the sun distressed them and their feet could carry them no further. When he finally called a halt, the exhausted men collapsed onto the sand and fell into deep, unbroken sleep, entirely forgetting the disputes that had threatened to tear them apart.

The classical sirah says Juwayriyyah accepted Islam, that the Prophet married her, and that the companions then released their captives of Banu al-Mustaliq. Aishah's remark that she knew no woman who brought more blessing to her people is part of that account. The Hawazin delegation after Hunayn, and the return of their captives, is a different event and is not the source of this marriage.

references.title: The Holy Quran
references.author: Surah Al-Munafiqun (63:1–8)
references.notes: Divine revelation exposing the hypocrites, affirming Zayd ibn Arqam's report, and declaring that all honor belongs to Allah and His Messenger.

references.title: Sahih al-Bukhari
references.author: Imam Muhammad ibn Isma'il al-Bukhari (d. 256 AH)
references.notes: Jabir: the quarrel, 'Leave it, for it is foul,' Ibn Ubayy's saying that the more honored would expel the meaner, and the Prophet's refusal to have him killed lest people say Muhammad kills his companions. The old span 4900–4907 was not cited number by number. Bukhari 4138 is the Mustaliq expedition but concerns a different question, so it is not cited for this scene.

references.title: Al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah
references.author: Ibn Hisham (d. 218 AH)
references.notes: The marriage to Juwayriyyah and the release of the captives are the classical sirah. Bukhari 2584 was removed. It concerns Hawazin after Hunayn, not this expedition, and it is not in the Book of Dutifulness.
